transcript.author: joan-martinez-alier

transcript.author: bruno-latour

transcript.author: michael-shellenberger
transcript.text: Reply to Anders and Jonas on waste: nuclear waste is small in volume, solid and fully contained, and France already manages it. interviews.author: michael-shellenberger
interviews.reaction: France should build new reactors. Dense, reliable, low-carbon power drove fossil fuels out of its grid, uses little land, and makes prosperity compatible with nature. The fear of nuclear waste and scarcity politics do more harm than the reactors do.

interviews.author: hans-jonas
interviews.reaction: I oppose. Reactors put irreversible harm on generations who cannot consent, and the bad prognosis should weigh more than the good one. Warming is also a grave risk, so the first duty is to cut demand, not to stake the future on one technology.

interviews.author: james-lovelock
interviews.reaction: I endorse it. Warming is the irreversible danger. It is too late for gentle sustainable development, and a planned retreat needs abundant low-carbon power. France has shown that fission works at scale. Its waste is small, stays in one place and can be guarded.

interviews.author: francoise-deaubonne
interviews.reaction: I oppose new reactors. Exhausting the earth and subjecting women come from the same patriarchal drive for centralised power and endless growth. Reactors cut carbon but feed that drive. The remedy is to take back control of production and of fertility.

interviews.author: andre-gorz
interviews.reaction: I oppose it. Nuclear power needs centralised, expert-run, policed control, so it takes energy choices away from the people affected. Ecology means a world people can understand and govern, starting from a shared norm of enough, not from ever more supply.

interviews.author: andreas-malm
interviews.reaction: I conditionally endorse new reactors. Warming comes from fossil capital, not from any particular technology, so reactors help only if they come with a political decision to shut down coal, oil and gas under public control.

interviews.author: serge-latouche
interviews.reaction: I oppose. New reactors treat demand as fixed and keep the religion of growth going. They rely on uranium mined elsewhere and on central expert control. First reduce, relocalise and redistribute, so that a frugal society needs far less power.

interviews.author: murray-bookchin
interviews.reaction: I oppose. New reactors keep energy in the hands of the state and a few firms, and that hierarchy is the social root of the ecological crisis. Energy should be decentralised and run by federated municipal assemblies.

interviews.author: joan-martinez-alier
interviews.reaction: I oppose new reactors as the claim is posed. Low-carbon accounting hides the conflicts along the uranium chain and at waste sites, where poor and colonised communities bear the burdens. They are owed a say and a debt.

interviews.author: malcom-ferdinand
interviews.reaction: I oppose the claim as posed, reasoning by analogy. French low-carbon power rests on uranium extracted abroad and waste kept beside marginalised communities. That repeats colonial inhabitation. No energy choice is just until those left ashore share the deck and the decision.

interviews.author: arne-naess
interviews.reaction: I oppose with a qualification. New reactors answer the shallow question of how to supply more power with less carbon. The deep question is why France needs so much energy. Centralised, expert-run technology also undermines local self-reliance.

interviews.author: bill-devall
interviews.reaction: I oppose. New reactors are reform environmentalism. They switch energy sources but keep the worldview that treats nature as a resource for growing demand. The deeper task is to need less, living simple in means and rich in ends.

interviews.author: timothy-morton
interviews.reaction: Neither yes nor no. Reactors swap one hyperobject, warming, for another, waste that lasts millennia. There is no away and no pristine Nature to return to, so any choice must accept caring for what it leaves behind indefinitely.

interviews.author: stewart-brand
interviews.reaction: Judge reactors by their measured effects on the climate. France's nuclear grid is already low-carbon, so new reactors should be built and fossil plants closed alongside them. Real waste and siting concerns call for careful management, not refusal.

interviews.author: jacques-ellul
interviews.reaction: I oppose. A reactor fleet is not a neutral tool. It calls for a centralised grid, permanent security and expert rule. It is sold on its low-carbon benefits while the problems it will create go unmentioned, so technique decides in place of politics.

interviews.author: gunther-anders
interviews.reaction: I oppose new reactors. Their dangers and waste last far longer than anyone can imagine or feel responsible for. Building more widens the gap between what we can make and what we can grasp, and low-carbon accounting does not close that gap.

interviews.author: jean-baptiste-fressoz
interviews.reaction: Energy sources have always been added to one another and have never replaced each other. New reactors cut emissions only if France also decides to close specific fossil uses on a fixed timetable. Without that decision, reactors just add capacity.

interviews.author: bruno-latour
interviews.reaction: I endorse it only on conditions. Reactors are assemblies of rivers, mines, waste and people. Build them if every one of these gets a spokesperson and France commits to caring for what it makes for millennia, rather than abandoning it.

interviews.author: starhawk
interviews.reaction: I oppose new reactors. They turn energy into power-over: centralised control, guarded sites, expert command and waste that binds future generations. Climate safety should come from power shared, through local renewable energy that communities can understand and govern themselves.

interviews.author: lewis-mumford
interviews.reaction: I oppose the claim. A reactor fleet is authoritarian technics: centralised, run by experts, guarded by the state and beyond its users' control. Electricity's real promise was a dispersed regional industry that communities can understand and govern.

interviews.author: giorgos-kallis
interviews.reaction: I oppose. The claim treats energy demand as fixed and only asks which source should feed growth. A society that sets its own limits would cut demand and share energy fairly first. Reactors built to keep growth going would tie France to that path for decades.

interviews.author: johan-rockstrom
interviews.reaction: I endorse it with conditions. Low-carbon power helps keep humanity inside the climate boundary, but only if fossil plants close as reactors open. New reactors also have to be judged against the other boundaries, including freshwater and novel entities.

interviews.author: isabelle-stengers
interviews.reaction: I oppose the claim as posed. A reactor fleet decided in a hurry, in the name of urgency, cuts out everyone it affects, human and not. Slow the decision down until rivers, miners, neighbours and future guardians of the waste have been able to object.

interviews.author: ted-nordhaus
interviews.reaction: France should build new reactors. Dense, abundant, low-carbon power lets human welfare grow while using less land, and offering investment and prosperity wins more support than a politics of limits.

interviews.author: robyn-eckersley
interviews.reaction: My support is conditional and leans slightly against. New reactors are acceptable only if the decision is democratic and answers to everyone affected. That includes future generations who inherit the waste, neighbouring countries, and the communities where uranium is mined. A closed technocratic programme fails that test.

interviews.author: bernard-charbonneau
interviews.reaction: I oppose the claim. A reactor fleet saves the climate by organising the whole country under central, expert and police control. Protecting nature through total management destroys the freedom that defending nature was meant to protect.

interviews.author: robert-bullard
interviews.reaction: Reactors are neither good nor bad in themselves. The test is distributive. France fails it if uranium mining, waste storage and risk land on poor, rural or colonised communities that had no real say in the decision.

interviews.author: kohei-saito
interviews.reaction: I oppose. New reactors keep production growing on a cleaner fuel and leave the metabolic rift open through mining and waste. Abundance comes from the commons, from free time and from producing less, not from new supply for capital.
